fields.definition: Magnetic recording tape whose formulation delivers a lower playback signal (output flux) for a given recorded level than standard or high-output stock, leaving less headroom before saturation and a poorer signal-to-noise ratio at a fixed reference fluxivity.
fields.plain_english: A kind of recording tape that gives back a weaker signal than newer, hotter tapes. Because the signal is weak, you must turn it up more, so you also hear more hiss and get less room before the sound distorts.
fields.purpose_function: Like any tape it stores recorded audio, but its lower sensitivity forces more playback gain that raises the noise floor, so recognizing it guides level, calibration, and noise-reduction choices during a transfer.
fields.practical_application: When transferring an older archive reel, a mastering engineer calibrates the machine to the tape's own reference level and applies extra make-up gain while watching the raised hiss floor.
common_mistakes: Assuming every reel has the same output and skipping calibration to the tape's own reference level
Adding heavy playback gain without accounting for the noise floor it raises
Mistaking a naturally low-output formulation for a worn or degraded tape
scenario_contexts: Transferring a vintage archive reel that reads several dB below a modern reference tape
Setting playback and calibration levels before digitizing an old master
Deciding how much noise reduction a hissy low-output transfer needs

sources: Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (magnetic recording chapter)
AES standards on magnetic tape reference fluxivity
Katz, Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science

fields.definition: The formal sign-off step in which a reference produced by the replication or duplication plant — such as a vinyl test pressing, a CD check disc, or a verified DDP image — is evaluated and accepted before full mass production begins.
fields.plain_english: The last 'yes, go ahead' check before a factory makes thousands of copies. Someone plays a sample made by the plant and confirms it sounds right before the full run starts.
fields.purpose_function: It catches errors the plant may add, such as clicks, wrong track order, or level faults, before the cost of a full run, protecting release quality and budget.
fields.practical_application: A mastering engineer or label representative auditions the plant's test pressing or check disc against the approved master, then signs off or requests a new one before the run.
common_mistakes: Approving from the studio master instead of the plant's actual reference copy
Skipping a full front-to-back listen and missing clicks or track-order errors
Confusing manufacturing approval with the client's earlier master approval
scenario_contexts: Auditioning a vinyl test pressing before authorizing the pressing run
Verifying a CD check disc against the DDP before glass mastering
Rejecting a test pressing for surface noise and requesting a recut

sources: Philips/Sony Compact Disc (Red Book) system description
Katz, Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science

fields.definition: The final, production-ready deliverable handed to a replication or duplication plant as the exact source for making copies — for CD a DDP image or PMCD, for vinyl a cut lacquer or approved digital cut file, and for digital release the encoded delivery files.
fields.plain_english: The finished copy of the audio that the factory uses to make every disc. It is the exact master template that all copies are stamped from.
fields.purpose_function: It gives the plant one authoritative, error-checked source so every manufactured copy matches the approved master exactly.
fields.practical_application: After mastering and approval, the engineer builds the manufacturing master, such as a DDP fileset with checksums, and delivers it to the plant for replication.
common_mistakes: Sending a rough or unapproved bounce instead of the final approved master
Omitting checksums so the plant cannot verify the delivered image
Confusing the manufacturing master with a personal reference or listening copy
scenario_contexts: Rendering a DDP image with checksums for a CD pressing plant
Delivering an approved digital cut file to a vinyl cutting house
Supplying encoded delivery files to a distributor for digital release

sources: Philips/Sony Compact Disc (Red Book) system description; DDP specification

fields.definition: The stage at which the client — artist, producer, or label — reviews the completed master and formally accepts it as final before it proceeds to manufacturing or release.
fields.plain_english: When the artist or label listens to the finished master and agrees it is done. Nothing goes to the factory until they give this approval.
fields.purpose_function: It confirms the master meets the client's creative and technical expectations and creates a clear point of agreement before any costly manufacturing steps.
fields.practical_application: The mastering engineer sends reference files, collects feedback, makes any revisions, and only releases the master for manufacturing once the client signs off.
common_mistakes: Sending a master to the plant before the client has approved it
Treating vague verbal comments as formal approval
Confusing the client's master approval with the plant's manufacturing approval
scenario_contexts: Emailing reference MP3s and awaiting the artist's sign-off before delivery
Holding manufacturing until label approval is confirmed in writing
Booking a revision when the client withholds approval over a level concern

sources: Katz, Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science

fields.definition: A finished master prepared and formatted specifically to serve as the source for making copies, with the track order, spacing, metadata, and format required by the copying process in place.
fields.plain_english: A finished master set up so it can be copied cleanly. All the track order, gaps, and file details are ready for the copying stage.
fields.purpose_function: It ensures the copying stage starts from a correctly formatted, error-checked source so every copy is faithful to the approved master.
fields.practical_application: Before delivery, the engineer sequences the songs, sets gaps and fades, embeds metadata, and exports the master in the format the copy house requires.
common_mistakes: Leaving track spacing, fades, or metadata unset before delivery
Delivering in a format the copy house cannot accept
Confusing simple duplication with pressed replication from a glass master
scenario_contexts: Sequencing and gapping an album before exporting a delivery fileset
Embedding ISRC and title metadata into a CD master
Preparing a verified fileset for a short-run CD-R duplication order

sources: Philips/Sony Compact Disc (Red Book) system description
Katz, Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science

fields.definition: The ordered series of processing stages a mix passes through during mastering — typically some combination of equalization, dynamics processing such as compression, harmonic or stereo-width processing, metering, and final peak limiting with dithering.
fields.plain_english: The line-up of tools the finished mix runs through in order during mastering. Each tool, such as EQ or a limiter, does one job before passing the sound to the next.
fields.purpose_function: It shapes tone, controls dynamics, and sets final loudness in a deliberate order so the finished master translates well across playback systems.
fields.practical_application: An engineer arranges processors so, for example, corrective EQ precedes compression and a limiter sits last, then tunes each stage while listening to the whole chain.
common_mistakes: Placing the limiter early so later processing overshoots the ceiling
Stacking heavy processing at every stage and crushing the dynamics
Ignoring gain staging so levels drift between devices in the chain
scenario_contexts: Ordering EQ, compression, and a limiter for an album master
Comparing an analog outboard chain against an in-the-box plugin chain
Adjusting one stage in the chain while auditioning the full path

sources: Katz, Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science

fields.definition: A new version of a master produced after the client requests changes, adjusting elements such as level, tone, spacing, or fades in response to feedback on a prior version.
fields.plain_english: An updated version of the master made after the artist or label asks for changes. The engineer tweaks things like loudness or tone and sends a fresh version.
fields.purpose_function: It lets the master be refined toward the client's goals through feedback while keeping earlier versions on record for comparison.
fields.practical_application: After a client notes a track is too bright, the engineer recalls the session, adjusts the EQ, exports a new labeled version, and sends it for review.
common_mistakes: Overwriting the previous version instead of saving a new labeled one
Making broad changes when only a small targeted tweak was requested
Losing track of which revision was actually approved
scenario_contexts: Brightening or darkening a track after client feedback
Rebalancing the level of one song relative to the album
Delivering a labeled version 2 master for a second round of review

sources: Katz, Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science

fields.definition: The working session in which a mastering engineer processes, sequences, and assembles final program material, along with the saved project file that stores its settings, edits, and track layout.
fields.plain_english: The work session where the engineer polishes and lines up the finished songs. It is also the saved project file that remembers all the settings and edits.
fields.purpose_function: It holds all processing, sequencing, and edit decisions in one recallable place so work can be reviewed, revised, and reproduced later.
fields.practical_application: The engineer loads mixes into the session, sets processing and song order, exports the master, and saves the session so revisions can be recalled exactly.
common_mistakes: Not saving the session, so a later revision cannot be recalled
Mislabeling versions and losing track of the approved state
Leaving mixes at inconsistent levels before starting to process
scenario_contexts: Assembling and sequencing an album in one session
Recalling a saved session to make a requested revision
Exporting the final master and DDP from the session

sources: Katz, Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science

fields.definition: The complete route audio takes through a mastering system, from the playback source through converters, patching, and the processing devices to the capture or output stage, including the monitoring feed used to judge it.
fields.plain_english: The full path the sound travels through the mastering gear, from the source, through the converters and processors, to where it is captured. It also covers the feed to the speakers you judge it on.
fields.purpose_function: It defines every point the signal passes so the engineer can keep the path clean, correctly leveled, and free of unwanted conversion or noise.
fields.practical_application: An engineer traces the path from converter to processors to capture, checking gain staging and connections so nothing adds noise or overload along the way.
common_mistakes: Confusing the whole signal path with just the processing chain
Overlooking a gain-staging error where the path crosses converters
Leaving an unused device inline that adds noise to the path
scenario_contexts: Tracing audio from the DAC through outboard gear back to capture
Diagnosing added noise by checking each point in the path
Verifying the monitoring feed matches the processed path being captured

sources: Katz, Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science
